claim: Pyroptosis and apoptosis are two forms of regulated cell death that can defend against intracellular infection.
source: Pyroptosis and apoptosis are two forms of regulated cell death that can defend against intracellular infection.
evidence: This is a general statement about the defensive roles of pyroptosis and apoptosis, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of immunology.

claim: When a cell fails to complete pyroptosis, backup pathways will initiate apoptosis.
source: When a cell fails to complete pyroptosis, backup pathways will initiate apoptosis.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing apoptosis activation in pyroptosis-deficient cells, and by citations to prior literature on backup apoptotic pathways.

claim: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium was previously engineered to persistently express flagellin, thereby activating NLRC4 during systemic infection in mice.
source: We previously engineered Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium to persistently express flagellin, and thereby activate NLRC4 during systemic infection in mice.
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors and is supported by citations to their previous publications (Miao et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2010a).

claim: The resulting pyroptosis clears flagellin-engineered S. Typhimurium.
source: The resulting pyroptosis clears this flagellin-engineered strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2) and by citations to prior publications.

claim: Infection of caspase-1 or gasdermin D deficient macrophages by flagellin-engineered S. Typhimurium induces apoptosis in vitro.
source: We now show that infection of caspase-1 or gasdermin D deficient macrophages by this flagellin-engineered S. Typhimurium induces apoptosis in vitro.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, including western blots and microscopy images demonstrating apoptotic markers.

claim: S. Typhimurium was engineered to translocate the pro-apoptotic BH3 domain of BID, which triggers apoptosis in macrophages in vitro.
source: Additionally, we engineered S. Typhimurium to translocate the pro-apoptotic BH3 domain of BID, which also triggers apoptosis in macrophages in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3, demonstrating the construction and apoptosis-inducing activity of the BIDON strain.

claim: During mouse infection, the apoptotic pathway successfully cleared engineered S. Typhimurium from the intestinal niche but failed to clear the bacteria from the myeloid niche in the spleen or lymph nodes.
source: During mouse infection, the apoptotic pathway successfully cleared these engineered S. Typhimurium from the intestinal niche but failed to clear the bacteria from the myeloid niche in the spleen or lymph nodes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse infections shown in Figures 2, 5, and 7, demonstrating differential clearance in different tissue compartments.

claim: The pyroptotic pathway was beneficial in defense of both intestinal and myeloid niches.
source: In contrast, the pyroptotic pathway was beneficial in defense of both niches.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse infections shown in Figures 2 and 7, demonstrating clearance in both tissue compartments.

claim: Apoptosis is a non-lytic form of regulated cell death that does not inherently cause inflammation.
source: Apoptosis is a non-lytic form of RCD that does not inherently cause inflammation.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of apoptosis supported by scientific knowledge and citations (Czabotar et al., 2014; Nagata and Tanaka, 2017).

claim: Apoptosis can be initiated via intrinsic or extrinsic signals.
source: Apoptosis can be initiated via intrinsic or extrinsic signals (Czabotar et al., 2014; Nagata and Tanaka, 2017).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about apoptosis pathways supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The intrinsic apoptotic pathway is regulated by the BCL-2 family of proteins, which monitor the cell for signs of damage or stress.
source: The intrinsic pathway is regulated by the BCL-2 family of proteins, which monitor the cell for signs of damage or stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.

claim: Cellular stress leads to the activation of the pro-apoptotic subset of the BCL-2 family, called BH3-only proteins (e.g. BID).
source: Cellular stress leads to the activation of the pro-apoptotic subset of this family, called BH3-only proteins (e.g. BID).
evidence: This is established knowledge about apoptotic signaling pathways.

claim: When activation signals overcome inhibition by anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members (e.g. BCL-2, MCL-1), it leads to assembly of BAK and/or BAX that form pores on mitochondria.
source: When these activation signals overcome inhibition by the anti-apoptotic subset of this family (e.g. BCL-2, MCL-1), it leads to assembly of BAK and/or BAX that form pores on mitochondria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of intrinsic apoptosis.

claim: Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) leads to the release of cytochrome c.
source: The resulting mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) leads to the release of cytochrome c.
evidence: This is established knowledge about apoptotic signaling, and is also demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C and Figure 3F.

claim: Cytochrome c initiates the formation of the apoptosome, activating caspase-9, which in turn cleaves and activates caspase-3, the prototypical executioner for apoptosis.
source: Cytochrome c initiates the formation of the apoptosome, activating caspase-9, which in turn cleaves and activates caspase-3, the prototypical executioner for apoptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the apoptotic signaling cascade.

claim: Caspase-9 and caspase-3 also activate caspase-7, which can cleave many of the caspase-3 target proteins that drive apoptosis.
source: Caspase-9 and –3 also activate caspase-7, which can cleave many of the caspase-3 target proteins that drive apoptosis, but whose unique function is to hyperactivate membrane repair (Nozaki et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent publication (Nozaki et al., 2022b).

claim: The unique function of caspase-7 is to hyperactivate membrane repair.
source: Caspase-9 and –3 also activate caspase-7, which can cleave many of the caspase-3 target proteins that drive apoptosis, but whose unique function is to hyperactivate membrane repair (Nozaki et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent publication by the authors (Nozaki et al., 2022b).

claim: Apoptosis can be activated by cell-extrinsic pathways through death receptors (e.g. FAS, TNFR1), which leads to the activation of caspase-8.
source: Apoptosis can also be activated by cell-extrinsic pathways through death receptors (e.g. FAS, TNFR1), which in turn leads to the activation of caspase-8 (Czabotar et al., 2014; Nagata and Tanaka, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about extrinsic apoptotic pathways, supported by citations.

claim: Caspase-8 can cleave BID.
source: These signaling pathways can reinforce each other, as caspase-8 can also cleave BID.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cross-talk between apoptotic pathways.

claim: Caspase-3 cleaves numerous substrates that together convert a cell into apoptotic bodies.
source: Caspase-3 then cleaves numerous substrates that together convert a cell into apoptotic bodies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the execution phase of apoptosis.

claim: Pyroptosis is a lytic, inherently inflammatory form of regulated cell death typically initiated by inflammasomes.
source: In contrast, pyroptosis is a lytic, inherently inflammatory form of RCD typically initiated by inflammasomes, which detect signs of infection within the cytosolic compartment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pyroptosis, supported by citations (Jorgensen et al., 2017; Nozaki et al., 2022a).

claim: Some inflammasomes directly detect microbial molecules, including proteins, LPS, or DNA; other inflammasomes indirectly detect the cytosolic perturbations caused by toxins.
source: Some inflammasomes directly detect microbial molecules, including proteins, LPS, or DNA; other inflammasomes indirectly detect the cytosolic perturbations caused by toxins (Jorgensen et al., 2017; Nozaki et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about inflammasome activation mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: NLRC4 can detect the activity of bacterial type III secretion systems when they aberrantly inject flagellin, rod, or needle proteins.
source: For example, NLRC4 can detect the activity of bacterial type III secretion systems when they aberrantly inject flagellin, rod, or needle proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NLRC4 inflammasome activation.

claim: Flagellin, rod, and needle proteins are directly detected via NAIP5/6, NAIP2, and NAIP1, respectively.
source: These are directly detected via NAIP5/6, NAIP2, and NAIP1, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NAIP-NLRC4 inflammasome specificity.

claim: NLRC4 can signal directly to caspase-1 to initiate pyroptosis, or indirectly via the ASC adaptor.
source: NLRC4 can signal directly to caspase-1 to initiate pyroptosis, or indirectly via the ASC adaptor (encoded by Pycard).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NLRC4 signaling pathways.

claim: ASC facilitates enhanced caspase-1 activation and is necessary for caspase-1 to efficiently cleave the cytokines pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature forms.
source: ASC facilitates enhanced caspase-1 activation and is necessary for caspase-1 to efficiently cleave the cytokines pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature forms (Broz et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Broz et al., 2010b).

claim: After NLRC4 activation, the direct activation of caspase-1 results in gasdermin D cleavage and activation without a requirement for ASC.
source: However, after NLRC4 activation, the direct activation of caspase-1 results in gasdermin D cleavage and activation without a requirement for ASC (Broz et al., 2010b; Kovacs and Miao, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Broz et al., 2010b; Kovacs and Miao, 2017).

claim: Cleaved gasdermin D forms a pore on the cell membrane, which is large enough to release mature IL-1β and IL-18 from the cell and to cause pyroptosis.
source: Cleaved gasdermin D then forms a pore on the cell membrane, which is large enough to release mature IL-1β and IL-18 from the cell and to cause pyroptosis (Xia et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gasdermin D function, supported by citation (Xia et al., 2021).

claim: There is cross-talk between apoptotic and pyroptotic pathways.
source: While apoptosis and pyroptosis are caused by distinct signaling events, there is nevertheless cross-talk between these pathways.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in the manuscript and by established knowledge in the field.

claim: If downstream pyroptotic signaling is inhibited, the cell will undergo apoptosis instead via backup pathways.
source: For example, there are distinct nodes where pyroptotic signaling proteins can also initiate apoptotic signaling. If downstream pyroptotic signaling is then inhibited, the cell will undergo apoptosis instead.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and by established knowledge about backup apoptotic pathways.

claim: ASC can recruit caspase-8.
source: The most apical node is ASC, which can recruit caspase-8 (Pierini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pierini et al., 2012.

claim: Caspase-1 can activate two different backup apoptosis pathways – by cleaving BID and by cleaving caspase-7.
source: Below this, caspase-1 can activate two different backup apoptosis pathways – by cleaving BID (Guégan et al., 2002; Heilig et al., 2020; Tsuchiya et al., 2019) and by cleaving caspase-7 (Lamkanfi et al., 2008; Mahib et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: When caspase-7 is activated in the absence of pores it might result in a partial form of apoptosis.
source: Although we propose that the primary function of caspase-7 is to drive membrane repair (Nozaki et al., 2022b), when it is activated in the absence of pores it might result in a partial form of apoptosis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the authors' prior work.

claim: Many intracellular bacteria have evolved mechanisms to evade detection by inflammasomes.
source: Many intracellular bacteria have evolved mechanisms to evade detection by inflammasomes (Jorgensen et al., 2017; Lacey and Miao, 2020; Maltez and Miao, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Backup apoptosis could restore cell death in the case of bacteria that inhibit pyroptosis.
source: Therefore, backup apoptosis could restore cell death in the case of bacteria that inhibit pyroptosis (Luchetti et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation and inference.

claim: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium encodes two distinct T3SS apparati.
source: To evade detection by inflammasomes, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium encodes two distinct T3SS apparati.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Salmonella biology.

claim: The Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI1) T3SS is used to invade epithelial cells.
source: The Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI1) T3SS is used to invade epithelial cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Salmonella pathogenesis.

claim: The flagellin that is co-expressed with SPI1 is detected by NLRC4, as are the SPI1 rod and needle proteins, albeit less efficiently.
source: However, the flagellin that is co-expressed is detected by NLRC4, as are the SPI1 rod and needle proteins, albeit less efficiently (Jorgensen et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NLRC4 detection is protective for the host in a mouse gastroenteritis model by reducing S. Typhimurium intracellular burdens.
source: This detection is protective for the host in a mouse gastroenteritis model by reducing S. Typhimurium intracellular burdens (Broz et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Broz et al., 2010a.

claim: Once S. Typhimurium has successfully invaded a cell and occupies the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV), it represses SPI1 and instead expresses SPI2.
source: Once S. Typhimurium has successfully invaded a cell and occupies the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV), it represses SPI1 and instead expresses SPI2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Salmonella intracellular gene expression.

claim: The SPI2 T3SS evades detection by NLRC4 via mutations on its rod proteins and by repressing flagellin expression.
source: The SPI2 T3SS evades detection by NLRC4 via mutations on its rod proteins and by repressing flagellin expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Salmonella immune evasion strategies.

claim: SPI2 evasion of NLRC4 permits intracellular replication in epithelial cells and macrophages.
source: This evasion permits intracellular replication in epithelial cells and macrophages (Broz et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: During the SPI2-driven intracellular phase, S. Typhimurium can be engineered to activate NLRC4 by expressing FliC under a SPI2 promoter (FliCON).
source: We previously demonstrated that during this SPI2-driven intracellular phase, S. Typhimurium can be engineered to activate NLRC4. This was accomplished by expressing the NLRC4 agonist FliC under a SPI2 promoter, herein called FliCON (Miao et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' prior publications.

claim: FliCON S. Typhimurium are detected by NLRC4 during the intracellular phase both in vitro and in vivo.
source: FliCON S. Typhimurium are detected by NLRC4 during the intracellular phase both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to prior publications.

claim: NLRC4 detection of FliCON results in the clearance of FliCON during systemic mouse infection.
source: This detection results in the clearance of FliCON during systemic mouse infection (Jorgensen et al., 2017; Jorgensen and Miao, 2015; Miao et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 and citations to prior publications.

claim: Pyroptosis is extremely detrimental to S. Typhimurium during intracellular replication, which is why S. Typhimurium normally represses flagellin.
source: This illustrates that the reason why S. Typhimurium normally represses flagellin is that pyroptosis is extremely detrimental to the bacterium during intracellular replication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing clearance of FliCON bacteria.

claim: FliCON S. Typhimurium is useful as an experimental tool to investigate the effectiveness of pyroptosis in vivo.
source: Furthermore, FliCON S. Typhimurium is useful as an experimental tool with which to investigate the effectiveness of pyroptosis in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the experimental system developed by the authors.

claim: Nlrc4–/– BMMs did not activate either pyroptotic or backup apoptotic pathways when infected with FliCON.
source: As a negative control, Nlrc4–/– BMMs did not activate either pyroptotic or backup apoptotic pathways (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Casp1–/– BMMs retain the ASC to caspase-8 pathway and show weak caspase-8, BID, and caspase-3 cleavage at 4 hr post-infection with FliCON.
source: Casp1–/– BMMs retain the ASC to caspase-8 pathway; and indeed, we observed weak caspase-8, BID, and caspase-3 cleavage at 4 hr post-infection (hpi) (Figure 1D), indicating that this pathway is relatively slow.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gsdmd–/– BMMs remain competent for both the ASC to caspase-8 and the caspase-1 to BID pathways and show stronger cleavage of BID, caspase-9, and caspase-3 than Casp1–/– BMMs.
source: In contrast, Gsdmd–/– BMMs remain competent for both the ASC to caspase-8 and the caspase-1 to BID pathways; and indeed, we observed stronger cleavage of BID, caspase-9, and caspase-3 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gsdmd–/– BMMs showed stronger caspase-8 cleavage compared to Casp1–/– BMMs, perhaps due to the ability of active caspase-3 and –7 to cleave caspase-8 in a feed-forward loop.
source: We also noticed stronger caspase-8 cleavage in the Gsdmd–/– BMMs compared to the Casp1–/– BMMs (Figure 1D), perhaps due to the ability of active caspase-3 and –7 to cleave caspase-8, in a feed-forward loop (Inoue et al., 2009; McComb et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and citations to prior literature explaining the mechanism.

claim: Only Gsdmd–/– BMMs displayed release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria to the cytosol during FliCON infection.
source: Further, only Gsdmd–/– BMMs displayed release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria to the cytosol during infection (Figure 1C), as expected by faster signaling from caspase-1 to BID.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cleaved BID (tBID) localizes to the mitochondria in Gsdmd–/– BMMs infected with FliCON.
source: Indeed, we also observed cleaved BID (tBID) localization to the mitochondria (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pycard/Gsdmd–/– BMMs and Bid/Gsdmd–/– BMMs had slightly reduced cleavage of caspase-8, -9, and -3 compared to Gsdmd–/– BMMs.
source: Compared to Gsdmd–/– BMMs, Pycard/Gsdmd–/– BMMs and Bid/Gsdmd–/– BMMs had slightly reduced cleavage of caspase-8,–9, and –3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) as expected due to the loss of only one of the two apoptotic pathways in each double knockout.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WT BMMs showed strong cleavage of gasdermin D but only weak cleavage of BID and caspase-7, and lacked cleavage of caspase-9 and –3 during FliCON infection.
source: Interestingly, WT BMMs, which are competent for all apoptotic and pyroptotic pathways showed strong cleavage of gasdermin D but only showed weak cleavage of BID and caspase-7, and lacked cleavage of caspase-9 and –3 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that completion of pyroptosis precludes the apoptotic signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Completion of pyroptosis precludes the apoptotic signaling pathway.
source: Interestingly, WT BMMs, which are competent for all apoptotic and pyroptotic pathways showed strong cleavage of gasdermin D but only showed weak cleavage of BID and caspase-7, and lacked cleavage of caspase-9 and –3 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that completion of pyroptosis precludes the apoptotic signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing lack of apoptotic markers in WT BMMs that undergo pyroptosis.

claim: WT BMMs infected with FliCON showed rapid release of LDH consistent with pyroptosis.
source: WT BMMs showed rapid release of LDH consistent with pyroptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Nlrc4–/– BMMs infected with FliCON did not show toxicity over time.
source: In accordance with our western blot data (Figure 1C–D), Nlrc4–/– BMMs infected with FliCON did not show toxicity over time (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Casp1–/– BMMs do not show much LDH release over the course of 8 hpi with FliCON, despite showing weak caspase-3 cleavage by 4–6 hpi.
source: While Casp1–/– BMMs did show weak caspase-3 cleavage by 4–6 hpi (Figure 1D), they do not show much LDH release over the course of 8 hpi (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Gsdmd–/– BMMs showed early signs of loss of viability when compared to Casp1–/– BMMs during FliCON infection.
source: As before, Gsdmd–/– BMMs showed early signs of loss of viability when compared to Casp1–/– BMMs (Figure 1E), agreeing with prior publications with different agonists (Doerflinger et al., 2020; Tsuchiya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations to prior publications.

claim: Pycard/Gsdmd–/– BMMs and Bid/Gsdmd–/– BMMs showed reduced LDH release compared to Gsdmd–/– BMMs during FliCON infection.
source: Pycard/Gsdmd–/– BMMs and Bid/Gsdmd–/– BMMs showed reduced LDH release compared to Gsdmd–/– BMMs (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vector control infections showed no LDH release over time.
source: Vector control infections showed no LDH release over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: The several backup pathways that remain in a Gsdmd–/– BMM cause LDH release, albeit slower than pyroptosis.
source: These data indicate that the several backup pathways that remain in a Gsdmd–/– BMM cause LDH release, albeit slower than pyroptosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the LDH release data from multiple genotypes.

claim: Both WT and Gsdmd–/– BMMs infected with FliCON for 4 hr showed strong PI staining.
source: As expected, both WT and Gsdmd–/– BMMs infected with FliCON for 4 hr showed strong PI staining, whereas neither Nlrc4–/– nor Casp1–/– BMMs had a high number of PI positive cells (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Brightfield images of WT BMMs infected with FliCON showed clear pyroptotic morphology.
source: Brightfield images of BMMs infected with FliCON showed clear pyroptotic morphology in WT BMMs, whereas Gsdmd–/– BMMs showed clear apoptotic blebbing that co-stained for cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Gsdmd–/– BMMs infected with FliCON showed clear apoptotic blebbing that co-stained for cleaved caspase-3.
source: Brightfield images of BMMs infected with FliCON showed clear pyroptotic morphology in WT BMMs, whereas Gsdmd–/– BMMs showed clear apoptotic blebbing that co-stained for cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Casp1–/– BMMs cellular morphology showed early signs of rounding but no apoptotic bodies during FliCON infection.
source: Casp1–/– BMMs cellular morphology showed early signs of rounding but no apoptotic bodies, whereas Nlrc4–/– BMMs infected with FliCON have no difference in cellular morphology from the controls (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Nlrc4–/– BMMs infected with FliCON have no difference in cellular morphology from the controls.
source: Casp1–/– BMMs cellular morphology showed early signs of rounding but no apoptotic bodies, whereas Nlrc4–/– BMMs infected with FliCON have no difference in cellular morphology from the controls (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Engineered FliCON S. Typhimurium activates the apoptotic backup pathways in vitro in BMMs.
source: Therefore, engineered FliCON S. Typhimurium activates the apoptotic backup pathways in vitro in BMMs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: FliCON was progressively cleared in WT mice at a rate of ~10 fold per day compared to WT S. Typhimurium.
source: FliCON was progressively cleared in WT mice at a rate of ~10 fold per day compared to WT S. Typhimurium (Figure 2B–C), consistent with our prior publications that pyroptosis is sufficient to clear FliCON (Jorgensen et al., 2016b; Miao et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C and citations to prior publications.

claim: FliCON was not cleared in Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: FliCON was not cleared in Nlrc4–/– mice, as expected (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: FliCON was not cleared in Casp1–/– mice, even though they are sufficient for the ASC to caspase-8 apoptotic backup pathway.
source: However, FliCON was also not cleared in Casp1–/– mice (Figure 2B and E), even though they are sufficient for the ASC to caspase-8 apoptotic backup pathway (Miao et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and E.

claim: FliCON was not cleared in Gsdmd–/– mice that retain caspase-1 to BID, caspase-1 to caspase-7, and ASC to caspase-8 backup pathways.
source: Furthermore, FliCON was not cleared in Gsdmd–/– mice that retain caspase-1 to BID, caspase-1 to caspase-7, and ASC to caspase-8 backup pathways (Figure 2B and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and F.

claim: FliCON was not cleared in Pycard/Gsdmd–/– or Bid/Gsdmd–/– mice that retain fewer backup pathways.
source: Finally, FliCON was not cleared in Pycard/Gsdmd–/– or Bid/Gsdmd–/– mice that retain fewer backup pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: The lack of FliCON clearance in apoptosis-competent mice also held true in a higher dose 105 total CFU infection.
source: This lack of clearance also held true in a higher dose 105 total CFU infection (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Trending, but not statistically significant increases in vector control burdens were observed in Casp1–/– and Gsdmd–/– mice, which may reflect incomplete evasion of NLRC4 and NLRP3.
source: When examining only the burdens of the vector control, we observed trending, but not statistically significant increases in Casp1–/– and Gsdmd–/– mice, which may reflect incomplete evasion of NLRC4 and NLRP3 (Broz et al., 2010a; Man et al., 2014), but this detection of vector-containing WT S. Typhimurium is much less effective in clearance compared to FliCON engineered bacteria (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with inference about the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The apoptotic backup pathways are not sufficient to clear either a high or low dose S. Typhimurium infection from the spleen when pyroptotic signaling is blocked.
source: Therefore, the apoptotic backup pathways are not sufficient to clear either a high or low dose S. Typhimurium infection from the spleen when pyroptotic signaling is blocked.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: BIDON bacteria grew normally in LB media.
source: BIDON bacteria grew normally in LB media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In WT BMMs, BIDON caused caspase-3 cleavage, while a negative vector control without the BIDBH3 domain did not.
source: In WT BMMs, BIDON caused caspase-3 cleavage, while a negative vector control without the BIDBH3 domain did not (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The weaker HA band in SspH1SS-HA-BIDBH3 compared to SspH1SS-HA could be due to caspase-3 cleaving after aspartates within the HA tag.
source: The weaker HA band in SspH1SS-HA-BIDBH3 compared to SspH1SS-HA could be due to caspase-3 cleaving after aspartates within the HA tag, which can efficiently destroy the HA epitope.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for an observation in the western blot data.

claim: The fused SspH1SS-HA-BIDBH3 protein is detectable by western blot with both α-HA and α-BID antibodies.
source: The fused SspH1SS-HA-BIDBH3 protein is detectable by western blot with both α-HA and α-BID antibodies (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: SspH1SS-HA-BIDBH3 is similar in length to full-length endogenous BID (predicted 21 kDa and 20 kDa, respectively), and resolved as a thicker band or sometimes as a doublet at ~20 kDa.
source: Coincidentally, SspH1SS-HA-BIDBH3 is similar in length to full-length endogenous BID (predicted 21 kDa and 20 kDa, respectively), and resolved as a thicker band or sometimes as a doublet at ~20 kDa (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot data with explanation.

claim: BIDON induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria, followed by weak caspase-9 cleavage, resulting in both cleaved caspase-3 and –7, and weak caspase-8 cleavage.
source: BIDON induced release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria, followed by weak caspase-9 cleavage, resulting in both cleaved caspase-3 and –7, and weak caspase-8 cleavage (Figure 3E–F).
